# Core Java

**SOLID**

1. **Single Responsibility Principle (SRP) \-** Every Java class must perform a single functionality.  
   UserService only registers users, and NotificationService handles emails.

2. **Open-Closed Principle (OCP) \-** module be open for extension but closed for [modification.Eg](http://modification.Eg).  
    Eg. PaymentProcessor has processPayment(), so \> CreditCardPaymentProcessor/ UPIProcessor will extend it.

3. **Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP) \-**  
   **\-** Derived/child classes must be completely substitutable for their base classes  
   Eg. Subclasses should be replaceable without altering the behavior of the program. ( list & arraylist )  
   `Eg. VehicleWithDoors` should work where `Vehicle` works

4. **Interface Segregation Principle (ISP)  \-**   
   larger interfaces split into smaller ones, do not force any client to implement an interface which is irrelevant to them. **Clients should not be forced to depend on methods they do not use**  
   **interface RestaurantWorker { void cookFood(); void serveFood(); void cleanTable(); }**  
   **A Chef should only be responsible for cooking, not serving or cleaning.**

5. **Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP) \-**   
   use of abstractions to decouple high-level modules from low-level modules. High level modules should not depend on low level modules.   
   ( **Do not depend on concrete implementation**, rather depend on abstraction ) eg. 

| class CreditCardPayment {     void pay(double amount) {         System.out.println("Paid $" \+ amount \+ " using Credit Card.");     } } // PaymentService is directly dependent on the concrete CreditCardPayment class PaymentService {     private CreditCardPayment payment;     public PaymentService() {         this.payment \= new CreditCardPayment(); // ❌ Tight coupling     }     public void processPayment(double amount) {         payment.pay(amount);     } }  |
| :---- |

**Core Java**

**1\. Hashcode() and equals() contract**

* The equals() and hashCode() contract in Java is a set of rules that **ensure objects are compared correctly** and **placed in the right hash buckets.**  
* **equals() \- by default it compares Object by reference**. Should be overridden to compare object values.  
* **hashCode ()** **\-** returns an integer that uniquely identifies an object. Should be consistent with equals(). Should **Contract   \-**  **If two objects are equal,** their **hashCode() must** be the **same.**  
    **If two objects are not equal,** their **hashCode() can** be the **same / different.**  
  **Benefits \-** ensures that objects that are equal are placed in the same hash bucket.  
  \==  **compares objects by reference for objects, but by value for primitives.**

 **Garbage Collection**

* Java garbage collection is an automatic process that manages memory in the heap.  
* **Unreferenced objects** can be **deleted** to free up memory ( from heap memory )  
* **Finalize**: **Before Destroying an object, the GC calls the finalize() method to perform cleanup activities**. The method is defined in Object class.  
* Algo: **Mark and Sweep.**

* **Minor garbage collection:** Also known as **young generation** garbage collection, this is used to **collect and reclaim memory that is used by short-lived objects** (objects that are quickly created and discarded).  
    
* **Major garbage collection:** Also known as **old-generation** garbage collection, this is used to collect and **reclaim memory that is used by long-lived objects** (objects that survive multiple minor garbage collections and are promoted to the old generation).  
    
* **Full garbage collection:** During full garbage collection, **memories from all generations are collected and reclaimed**, including **memories of young and old**. A full garbage collection normally takes longer to complete than a minor or major garbage collection which causes that app to pause temporarily.

   
**Java Memory Management**   
**![][image3]**

Memory is split into two main sections: the **Heap** and the **Metaspace** (formerly known as PermGen starting from Java 8).

**MetaSpace \-**   
  Stores class metaData associated with loaded classes.( **Static variables** )  
  **Class Metadata** \- (method names, fields, modifiers, etc.).  
  **Constant Pool** \- Stores runtime constants, including method references, field names, and literals.  
    
 **`MetaspaceSize`** → Initial allocation.  
 **`MaxMetaspaceSize`** → Maximum allowed Metaspace size.

|  class  Example {                                                             static  int x \= 10;   // Stored in Metaspace                 String name;         // Stored in Heap (inside object)                                                                                          void display() {                                                                Int  local \= 5;   // Stored in Stack                             }                                                                                }           |
| :---- |

                
  ![][image4]                
![][image5]          
 **Heap**  
Consists of dynamically allocated memory where **objects are stored**. ( using “new” keyword )  
Also for **data structures like Arrays, Collections eg. new List()** ![][image6]                               
The heap is divided into two main areas:

**Young Generation**:  
This area is further divided into **Eden space and two Survivor spaces** (From and To). **Objects are initially allocated in the Eden space**. **When the Eden space becomes full, a minor garbage collection is triggered, and surviving objects are moved to one of the** **Survivor spaces S0 and S1**. Objects that survive multiple garbage collection cycles in the Survivor spaces are eventually promoted to the Old Generation.

**Old Generation**:  
This area is also known as the Tenured Generation. It is used to **store long-lived objects** that have **survived multiple garbage collection cycles** in the Young Generation. **Major garbage collections are performed in the Old Generation** to **reclaim memory from unreachable objects**.

The heap size can be adjusted using JVM flags such as **\-Xms (initial heap size)** and **\-Xmx (maximum heap size).** Proper tuning of the heap size is essential for optimizing the performance and stability of Java applications.

**Q. What are Memory Leaks ? How to resolve or prevent it ?**

When **objects are not properly garbage collected** and **continue to consume memory over time**. Identifying and fixing memory leaks prevents excessive memory consumption and potential OutOfMemoryError crashes  
**Track memory: Prometheus, Grafana, New Relic** in a centralized dashboard.

**Logging and Alerting:** Configure logging and alerting mechanisms to monitor memory usage thresholds and trigger alerts when memory usage exceeds predefined thresholds. Use logging frameworks like Log4j or SLF4J to log memory usage metrics.  
---

**Memory leaks \-**

- **when objects that are no longer needed remain referenced, preventing garbage collection and causing increased memory usage over time.**  
- **static** List\<String\> cache \= new ArrayList\<\>();  // **Objects never released** 

- **Open connections from stream.**  
- **FileInputStream fis** \= **new FileInputStream("file.txt");** // **If not closed, it may cause memory leaks**   
- **fis.close();**


- **Overuse of Caches (Maps Not Cleared)**  
- **Map\<Integer, String\> cache \= new HashMap\<\>();**  
- **cache.put(1, "data");  // If keys are never removed, memory will grow**

- **Opened DB connection**

**Serialization:**  
Serialization in Java is the process of converting an object into a byte stream so that it can be persisted to a file, database, or transmitted over a network. The reverse process, called **deserialization**, reconstructs the object from the byte stream.  
**Serializable**

**If a serialized object’s `serialVersionUID` does not match the current class version, an InvalidClassException occurs.**

* **Polymorphism \-**  Allowing multiple forms

    **   Compile-time** (Method Overloading) \- Same method name, different parameters

* **Abstraction \- Hiding implementation details** and exposing only essential features (e.g., interfaces, abstract classes).  
* **Encapsulation \-  encapsulating data and methods into a single unit like class.**  
  Hiding data using private variables inside a and exposing only necessary details via getters/setters.

**Abstract class vs Interface**  
 

| Abstract Class | Interface |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Both abstract and non-abstract method** | **Only Abstract methods** (default & static methods allowed after java 8\) |
| **Cannot be instantiated** | **No**  |
| No multiple class inheritance **(extends one class)** | Can **implement multiple interfaces** |
| **Can have any access modifier** | **Methods are `public` by default** |
| **Can have instance variables ( variables )** | **Only  public static final  constants** |

**When to use abstract methods \-** when we want the child class to decide the implementation in that case we use abstract methods.✔ Use **abstract class** when sharing **common behavior** across subclasses.

**Abstract class \-** cannot be instantiated **( object cannot be created )** may or may not contain abstract methods, if at least 1 abstract method then must declare the class as abstract.

**Tricky questions \-** 

#### **1\. Can a constructor be private?**

* **Yes**, used in **Singleton Pattern** to restrict object creation.

---

#### **2\. Can we override a static method?**

* **No**, because **static methods belong to the class**, not instances.  
* **Hiding** occurs if a subclass redefines a static method.

---

#### **3\. What is the `super` and `this` keyword?**

* **`super`** – Calls the parent class’s constructor / instance or method.  
* **`this`** – Refers to the current instance and calls the constructor of  the same class.

---

#### **4\. Can an abstract class have a constructor?**

* **Yes**, **an abstract class can have a constructor.** I**t is used to initialize common fields before subclass constructors are called.**

#### ---

#### **5\. Can we create an object of an abstract class?**

* **No**, but we can create an anonymous inner class instance of it.

#### ---

#### **6\. Can we override a private method?**

* **No**, because private methods are not inherited.

**5\.** **Streams API**

A stream is a **sequence of elements** that can be **processed in a functional style**.   
It is used to process collections of objects with the functional style **using the lambda expression. Different methods can be pipelined to produce desired outcome.**  
**Methods \-** filter(), forEach(), map(), flatMap(), collect(), reduce(), sorted()

The stream allows you to perform various operations like filtering, mapping, and reducing.  
The **`filter`** method is used to keep only those elements in the stream that match a given condition (predicate).

##  **1\. `Consumer<T>` (Takes Input, No Output)**

A **`Consumer<T>`** takes **one input** and **performs an action** but **does not return anything**.

List\<String\> names \= Arrays.asList("Alice", "Bob", "Charlie");  
**Consumer**\<String\> **printUpperCase** \= name \-\> System.out.println(name.toUpperCase()); names.forEach(**printUpperCase**); // ALICE, BOB, CHARLIE

## **2\. `Supplier<T>` (No Input, Returns Output)**

A **`Supplier<T>`** **does not take any input** but **returns a value**.

**Supplier**\<Integer\> **randomNumberSupplier** \= () \-\> new Random().nextInt(100); System.out.println(**randomNumberSupplier.get()**); // Random number between 0-99

## **3\. `Predicate<T>` (Takes Input, Returns Boolean)**

A **`Predicate<T>`** takes **one input** and **returns a boolean (`true` or `false`)**.

**Predicate**\<Integer\> **isEven** \= num \-\> num % 2 \== 0; // Lambda expression implementing the sum method // Lambda expression implementing the sum method  
System.out.println(isEven.test(10)); // true

**5\. Map vs Filter vs Reduce**

| Map | Filter  | Reduce |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Traverse and Transforms elements of list.** | **Filter’s ( select ) element based on the condition. ( predicate ), Remove unwanted elements.** | **Aggregates elements to a single value.** |
| Input: Stream\<T\> | Input: Stream\<T\> | Stream\<T\> |
| Output: Stream\<R\> | Stream\<T\> | T ( single value ) |
| Used for **modifying each element** **in the stream.**( eg. Data transformation ) | Used for **removing elements** that don't match a condition.( eg. conditional selection ) | Used for **reducing** stream elements into a single value. ( eg. Sum, max, min ) |

**8\. Map vs FlatMap** 

## **✅ 1\. `map()`**

* **Used for transformation (one-to-one mapping).**  
* **Takes an element and applies a function, returning a new Stream of transformed elements.**  
* **Does NOT flatten nested structures.**

## **✅ 2\. `flatMap()`**

* **Used for flattening nested structures (one-to-many mapping).**  
* It takes each element, applies a function, and **flattens the result** into a single Stream.

 

|  List\<String\> words \= List.of("Hello", "World");  // Using flatMap() to get a Stream\<Character\>  List\<Character\> result \= words.stream()                                            .flatMap(word \-\> word.chars().mapToObj(c \-\> (char) c))                                       .collect(Collectors.toList());  |
| :---- |

* Comparable**: Natural ordering** of objects, A class should implement this and **override compareTo().**  
  **(** which will compare the current obj with another obj of **same class** **)**

* Comparator**: Custom sorting** logic externally**.** Class **must override `compare().`**  
  `(` which compares two objects of the **same or different classes** ).  
  The **`compare()`** method returns the same values as **`compareTo()` (0, negative integer (-1), positive integer(+1)).**

**11\.  What is the difference between `final`, `finally`, and `finalize`?**

* **`final`: A keyword used to declare constants, prevent method overriding, and prevent class inheritance.**  
  * **`finally`: A block of code that is always executed after a `try` block, regardless of whether an exception is thrown.**  
  * **`finalize`: A method in the `Object` class that is called by the garbage collector before an object is reclaimed.**

**12\. Volatile**  
The volatile keyword is used to **declare variables that require visibility across threads**. When a variable is declared as volatile, **changes made to that variable are immediately visible to all threads**, and reads and writes to the variable are atomic.

**5\. Spring Boot @Component  vs @Service vs @Bean**

@component \- **Marks a class as a Spring-managed bean.**  
The Spring **container automatically detects and registers the annotated class as a bean using component scanning.**

@Service \- Indicates that a **class contains business logic** or service-layer code.  
Internally, `@Service` is just a specialization of `@Component`

@Bean \- **Denotes a method** that **explicitly defines a bean in the Spring configuration class.**  
Beans defined with `@Bean` are registered in the Spring IOC container.

**6\. HashMap** 

HashMap stores data in (**key**, **value**) pairs. Each key is associated with a value, and you can access the value by using the corresponding key. HashMap contains an **array of the nodes/buckets, It uses an Array and LinkedLists internally for storing Key and Value pairs.**

* **Not Synchronized** (unlike Hashtable in Java) and hence faster for most of the cases.  
* Duplicate Elements not allowed in HashMap**, if you try to insert the duplicate key in HashMap, it will replace the element of the corresponding key.**  
* HashMap allows for **efficient key-based retrieval**, **insertion**, and **removal** with average O(1) time complexity.  
  With capacity of 16 and load factor of 0.75.  
* **Allows to store the null keys** as well, but there should be only one null key object and there can be any number of null values. And it is **not ordered**.  
* Hashset also uses hashmap internally.


**Internal working:**  

* Internally HashMap contains an **array of Nodes / LinkedList** and node class contains 4 things.

| Int Hash | Key | Value | Node Next |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |

* **Buckets:** **Array of the node are called buckets**. Each node has a data structure like a LinkedList. More than one node can share the same bucket.

**![][image14]**

**Equals():** It **checks the equality of 2 objects.** It compares the Key, whether they are equal or not.   
**It is a method of Object class**. If you override the equals() method, then it is mandatory to override the hashCode() method.

**HashCode():** It is method of object class. **It returns the memory reference of the object in integer form,** This value is used as the bucket number, it is address of the element inside map. HashCode of **null key is 0\.**

**Internal working:** If we **map.put()** (“Prasad”, “26”), then the HashCode of “Prasad” is calculated eg. 223454, to store the key in memory we have to calculate index. The Formula is **Index \= hashcode(Key) & (n-1)  ..** here n=16  
Eg. index \= 4, then in that bucket the map entry will be stored.

**Hash Collision:** When index is same for 2 or more keys, In this case, equals() method checks that both Keys are equal or not. 

* **If Keys are same, replace the value with the current value**.   
* **Else connect this** **node object to the existing node object through the LinkedList.**

**Get()** Method in hashmap \-

* Used to get value by key.  
* Firstly HashCode of the key is calculated, then we get the index in array, Then each key is compared and if a match is found then value is returned.


  
**7\. HashMap Vs TreeMap**

**HashMap** \- **Hash table** (uses hashing to map keys to buckets)  
PerformanceAverage Case: O(1) for basic operations (get, put, containsKey)  
Worst Case: O(n) (if hash function is poorly designed and leads to many collisions)

**Database indexing**: Hashmaps can speed up data retrieval.  
**Caching**: Hashmaps can store and quickly retrieve the results of expensive computations.   
**Associative mapping**: Hashmaps can associate one value with another, such as mapping usernames to user profiles.

**TreeMap** \- **`TreeSet ->` Red-Black tree** (a self-balancing binary search tree) \- **Root node** is always black  
Performance: **O(log n)** for basic operations (get, put, containsKey)  
Usage: **When you need to iterate over elements in sorted order. Maintains orders.**   
**( It is sorted as per compareTo method overridden in the class )**

**23\. HashMap vs HashTable**

| HashMap | HashTable |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Not Synchronized** | **Synchronized** |

| **Iterator is used to traverse HashMap** | **Both Iterator and Enumerator are used** |
| **Faster** | **Slower** |

**24\. ArrayList**

**\-** Implemented as a **resizable array.**  
**\-** ArrayList is **not synchronized.**  
**\- High performance, Initial capacity of 10\.**  
**\- Preserve insertion order.**

Grows dynamically in size, **each element is stored in a sequential block of memory.** **default capacity is 10 elements,** ArrayList **elements are copied from original array to new array when the original array is full.** 

As the size increases the **class creates a new array of bigger sizes and it copies all elements from old array to new array,** now the **reference of the new array is used internally.**

**25\. ArrayList vs LinkedList**

| ArrayList | LinkedList |
| :---- | :---- |
| Implemented as **expandable array/ dynamic array** | Implemented as a **doubly linked list.** |
| **Elements are stored in contiguous memory locations,** Manipulation with ArrayList is slow because it internally uses an array. If any element is removed from the array, all the other elements are shifted in memory. | **Stored in non-contiguous way, as each element has reference to next and prev element.** Manipulation is faster like removing so no bit shifting is required in memory. |
| **Faster for random access ( search is faster )** | **Slow for random access ( search is slower )** |
| **Slower for inserting at start or middle** | **Faster for insertion and deletion.** |
| Memory efficient **Best for storing and accessing** | Less memory efficient**better for manipulating** |
| Can only **act as List** | Can act as **List and Queue**  |

**29\. Set**

Sets are **collections that don’t store duplicate elements. They don’t keep any order of the elements.** 

* **HashSet:**   
  **stores the elements in a hash table which provides faster lookups and faster insertion. HashSet is not ordered.**

* **LinkedHashSet:**   
  **LinkedHashSet is an implementation of HashSet in doubly linked list which maintains the insertion order of the elements.**

* **TreeSet:**   
  **stores the elements in a sorted order that is determined by the natural ordering of the elements or by a custom comparator provided at the time of creation.**

**30\. HashSet**

**\- Stores a collection of distinct elements.  Internally uses HashMap().** Each element is **mapped to an index** **in an array** of buckets using a **hash function**, and the index is used to quickly access the element. The hash function distributes the elements among the buckets based on the calculated index.   
\- **The element is stored as a key and the value is “PRESENT”.**

| Key | Value |
| :---- | :---- |
| **Element** | *Present* |

**37\. Static**  
The static keyword in Java is used to indicate that a particular field, method, or block of code belongs to the class, rather than instances of the class.

**Static Members:**  
 \- Shared among all instances of the class.f  
 \- Accessed using the class name (`ClassName.memberName`)

**Static Limitations:**  
\- Static methods cannot access non-static (instance) members directly.  
\- Use of `this` or `super` in static contexts is not allowed.

###     **Can we override the static method?**

\- No, as static methods are part of class rather than object.

**38\. Explain the difference between \== and .equals() in Java.**

**\==** operator is used to compare primitive data types and checks if two references point to the same object in memory, **equals()** method is used to compare the contents of two objects.

 **\==** Compares **references** for objects (whether they point to the same memory location).  
\- For **primitive types**, it compares actual values.

**equals()** Compares **contents** (logical equality) of objects.  
\- Needs to be overridden in custom classes to provide meaningful equality.

**2\. Structural**  
**\-** Structural design patterns focus on how classes and objects are arranged to create larger, more complex structures in software development.

**Decorator Method Design Pattern**  
It allows us to dynamically add functionality and behavior to an object without affecting the behavior of other existing objects within the same class.   
We use inheritance to extend the behavior of the class. This takes place at compile-time, and all the instances of that class get the extended behavior.

**3\. Behavioral**  
**\-** Group of design patterns that focus on how objects and classes interact and communicate in software development.

**Chain Of Responsibility Method Design Pattern**  
Chain of responsibility pattern is used to achieve loose coupling in software design where a request from the client is passed to a chain of objects to process them.   
Later, the object in the chain will decide themselves who will be processing the request and whether the request is required to be sent to the next object in the chain or not.

**Observer Method Design Pattern**  
It establishes a one-to-many dependency between objects, meaning that all of the dependents (observers) of the subject are immediately updated and notified when the subject changes.

# MultiThreading

**Multithreading** is a feature in Java that **allows concurrent execution of two or more parts** of a program to maximize CPU utilization. 

**What is a thread in Java?**

A **thread** is a small unit of a process that allows a program to perform multiple tasks concurrently. Multithreading is a Java feature that allows concurrent/parallel execution of two or more parts of a program for maximum utilization of CPU.

### **Creating Threads in Java:**

1. **Extending `Thread` Class**: Extend the `Thread` class and override the `run()` method. Code

2. **Using the `Runnable` Interface**: Implement the `Runnable` interface and define the `run()` method.

3. **Using Lambda Expressions (Java 8+)**: For shorter syntax with `Runnable code`

| Thread t \= new Thread( () \-\> { sout(“Thread is running” ) } ); t.start(); |
| :---- |

---

**Thread lifecycle**

A thread in Java at any point in time exists in any one of the following states. 

* **New**: The thread has been created but has not yet started.  
* **Runnable**: The thread is running, executing its task, or is ready to run if there are no other higher-priority threads.  
* **Blocked**: The thread is **temporarily suspended**, **waiting for a resource** or an event.  
* The thread **tries to access a locked resource** but must wait.  
* Example: Multiple threads trying to access a synchronized block.

* **Waiting**: The thread is **waiting for another thread to perform a task** or for a **specified amount of time** to elapse. The thread **waits indefinitely** for another thread to **notify it.**  
  **Sleep : Thread sleeps for 5 seconds**

| synchronized (this) {      wait(); // Moves to Waiting state until notify() is called }Thread.sleep(5000); |
| :---- |


* **Terminated**: The thread has **completed its task** or **been terminated by another thread.**  
  **![][image24]**

 **Sleep() Vs Wait() in MultiThreading**

**Sleep** \- Temporarily **pauses** the **current thread for a specified duration**. If the thread **holds lock** on a shared resource (e.g., within a synchronized block), the **lock is not released during sleep**. This can potentially block other threads from accessing the resource.  
After the specified sleep time elapses, the thread automatically resumes execution.

**Wait** \- Allows a thread to **temporarily suspend execution** and **release lock** on the object it's synchronized on.  
**Wakes up on notification:** The thread remains suspended until another thread notifies it using **`notify()`** or **`notifyAll()`** on the same object.  
![][image25]

**4\. Explain synchronized** keyword in Java.

The synchronized keyword in Java is used to **control the access of multiple threads to any shared resource.**  
It is used to **prevent thread interference** and consistency problems.   
Synchronization ensures that **only one thread** can access a shared resource at a time to avoid **race conditions**.

When we use **`synchronized (SingletonClass.class){ code }`**, we are acquiring a **class-level lock**, which ensures that only **one thread** can execute the synchronized block for this class at a time.

### **Class-Level Lock vs Instance-Level Lock**

* **`synchronized (this)`** → Locks the current **instance** of the object.  
* **`synchronized (SingletonClass.class)`** → Locks the **class itself**, meaning it applies to **all instances** of the class.

**public class SingletonClass {**  
   **private static volatile SingletonClass *instance*;**  
   **// Volatile ensures proper visibility across threads**

   **private SingletonClass() {}                    // Private constructor**

   **public static SingletonClass getInstance() {**  
       **if (*instance* \== null) {                   // First check (without locking)**  
           **synchronized (SingletonClass.class) { // Acquiring class-level lock**  
               **if (*instance* \== null) {           // Second check (inside lock)**  
                   ***instance* \= new SingletonClass();**  
               **}**  
           **}**  
       **}**  
       **return *instance*;**  
   **}**  
**}**

### **Why use `SingletonClass.class` instead of `this`?**

* **`this`** can only be used inside **instance methods**, but `getSynchronizedInstance2()` is a **static method**.  
* **`SingletonClass.class` ensures thread safety across all instances** of the class, making it suitable for singleton patterns.


**5\. Volatile**  
The volatile keyword is used to d**eclare variables that require visibility guarantees**. When a variable is declared as volatile, **changes made to that variable are immediately visible to all threads**, and reads and writes to the variable are atomic.

**6\. Deadlocks and how to avoid them ? ( Race condition )**  
A deadlock occurs when two or more threads are waiting for each other's resources indefinitely, preventing further execution.Nested synchronized blocks

### **Why Does This Cause Deadlock?**

1. **Thread 1 locks `A`** and waits for `B`.  
2. **Thread 2 locks `B`** and waits for `A`.  
3. Both threads are **waiting indefinitely**, causing a **deadlock**.

## **How to Avoid Deadlocks?**

### **1️⃣ Use a Consistent Locking Order**

* Always acquire locks in the **same order** across all threads.

### **What is a Race Condition?**

A **race condition** occurs when **multiple threads access shared data simultaneously** and **the final outcome depends on the execution order**.

## **How to Prevent Race Conditions?**

### **1️⃣ Use `synchronized` (Ensures Mutual Exclusion)**

2️⃣ Use **`AtomicInteger`** (Faster & Lock-Free)

**Use `Callable` when you need to:**

* **Perform computation and retrieve output asynchronously.**

### **Core Features in Spring Boot Microservices**

### **Advantages of Microservices in Spring Boot**

# Authentication

**JWT \-** (**JSON Web Token**) is a token-based authentication mechanism used in **stateless authentication**. Instead of storing session data on the server, a JWT is sent with each request to verify the user.

### **🛠 Key Components of JWT**

1. **Header** → Metadata about the token (e.g., algorithm used).  
2. **Payload (Claims)** → User data & custom claims.  
3. **Signature** → Used to verify the token’s authenticity.

**Steps :**

**1️⃣ User Logs In**  
The client (user) sends a login request with username & password.

### **2️⃣ Server Validates Credentials**

* The authentication server checks the username/password.  
* If valid, it **creates a JWT** containing the **user’s details** & **expiration time**.  
* The JWT is signed with a **secret key** to prevent tampering.

3️⃣ **Server Sends JWT to Client**

* The server returns the JWT in the response.  
* The client **stores the token** (e.g., local storage, session storage, or cookies).

4️⃣ **Client Sends JWT with Each Request**

* For every **protected API request**, the client **attaches the JWT** in the `Authorization` header.

### **5️⃣ Server Verifies JWT**

* The server **decodes the JWT**, verifies the signature, and checks expiration.  
* If valid, it processes the request and sends the response.  
* If the token is **invalid or expired**, the server returns **401 Unauthorized**.

![][image29]

**2\. Spring Authentication** 

**1\.  User Sends a Request**  
**\-** User/Client sends HTTP requests to a secured REST endpoint.  
**\-** It includes authentication credentials ( username/password or token ) in the Auth Header.

**2\. Spring Security Filters the Request**  
**\-** Request goes through spring security’s filter chain, ( checks if authentication is needed )  
**\-** eg. **JwtAuthenticationFilter** ( for token based authentication )

**3\.  AuthenticationManager Validates Credentials**  
**\-** Request is passed to an AuthenticationManager, which processes authentication.  
**\-** It delegates the check to one or more AuthenticationProvider implementations.  
\- Eg. **JWTAuthenticationProvider** validates JWT tokens.

**User authentication \-** 

**4\. UserDetailsService Fetches User Data**  
**\- If authentication involves a username/password**, **spring security** loads the user details using **UserDetailsService**.  
\- This service fetches user data from a database or other sources.

**5\. Password Verification**  
\- The provided password is **compared against the stored hashed password.**  
\- this is handled using a PasswordEncoder like **BcryptPasswordEncoder.**

**6\. Authentication success or failure**  
**\- If Succeeds: A SecurityContext is created and stored in SecurityContextHolder.**  
**\-**The user gains access to the requested resource

**Token Based Authentication ( JWT )**  
**\-** The server generates a JWT after successful login.  
\- The Client includes JWT tokens in the subsequent requests.  
\- **JwtAuthenticationFilter** extracts and validates the token.

 **Authorization (Role-Based Access Control)**  
**\-** Even if authentication is successful, spring security checks user roles  before allowing access to specific endpoints.

# Tricky Questions

## **1\. Why does Java not support multiple inheritance?**

### **Why this?**

* Multiple inheritance can introduce **diamond problem**, causing ambiguity in method resolution.

### **Why not allow multiple inheritance and handle conflicts explicitly?**

* It increases **code complexity**.

* Leads to **method resolution conflicts** that are hard to debug.

### **What are the benefits of Java’s approach?**

* Java uses **interfaces** and **default methods** (from Java 8\) to achieve multiple inheritance **without ambiguity**.

### **How does Java handle multiple inheritance via interfaces?**

* If two interfaces provide the same default method, the **implementing class must override it** explicitly.

![][image31]

## **Why does Java have the `volatile` keyword?**

* `volatile` ensures that **updates to a variable are always read from main memory.**  
* Prevents **visibility issues** in multithreading.  
* Does **not** provide atomicity (use `synchronized` or `Atomic variables` if needed).

### **Why not just use `synchronized` everywhere?**

* `synchronized` introduces **performance overhead** by blocking threads.

### **What are the benefits of `volatile`?**

* Ensures **visibility of updates across threads.**  
* **Lighter than synchronization**.

### **How does it work?**

* **Forces read/write from main memory** instead of CPU cache.

---

## **Why use `ReentrantLock` over `synchronized`?**

### **Why this?**

* `synchronized` has **limitations**, such as **lack of tryLock() and fair locking**.

### **Why not always use `synchronized`?**

* Cannot check lock status.

* No fairness control.

### **What are the benefits of `ReentrantLock`?**

* Supports **tryLock()** (non-blocking).

* Allows **fair locking** (FIFO order).

### **How does it work?**

* Uses **explicit lock() and unlock()** methods.

**Runnable vs Callable**

### **7\. What are WeakReferences and why use them?**

**Why this?** Managing memory efficiently.  
 **Why not?** \- **Overusing strong references can cause memory leaks.**  
 **Benefits?** \- **Weak references help in garbage collection.**  
 **How does it work?**

* **Strong Reference**: Prevents GC unless explicitly set to null.  
* **Weak Reference**: Allows GC when no strong references exist. Used in **caching mechanisms**.  
* `WeakReference<T>` allows objects to be collected when memory is low.  
* Used in conjunction with `ReferenceQueue` for cleanup.

**2\. IOC container ( \*\*\*VIP\*\*\* )**

* **Manages the lifecycle and dependencies of your application‘s objects** ( beans ).  
* **It follows the Dependency Injection (DI) principle**. **where objects do not create their dependencies but receive them from the container.**

**Inversion of Control:** Instead of your objects/class creating their dependencies, the container injects them. This reverses the traditional control flow. You describe *what* you need, not *how* to get it.  
**DI:** **Outsourcing the task of object creation**, which is a pattern that allows building decoupled systems.  
\- We do not create objects/instance of class, IOC container create and manage them for us.

**Application Context is implementation of spring IOC container.**  
   1\. **Creates and Manages Beans**  
   2\. **Dependency Injection**  
   3\. **Annotations used** \- **@Component**, **@Service**, **@Repository**, **@Controller** and **@Bean** register beans inside the container.

## **3.1 How to Define Profiles in Spring Boot?**

| server:   port: 8080 spring:   profiles:     active: dev  \# Set the active profile |

**3.2 Usage of @profiles**   
**(Switching Databases Based on Profile)**

|  @Configuration public class DatabaseConfig {     @Bean     @Profile("dev")     public DataSource h2DataSource() {         return new DataSource("jdbc:h2:mem:devdb", "sa", "");     }     @Bean     @Profile("prod")     public DataSource mySqlDataSource() {         return new DataSource("jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/prod\_db", "root", "securepassword");     } }  |
| :---- |

## **3.3 Spring Boot Profile Default Behavior**

**Setting active profile** \=\>  
1️⃣ Using **`application.properties`** `-` spring.profiles.active \= dev  
**2️⃣** Using **Command Line Arguments**    \-  java \-jar myapp.jar \--spring.profiles.active=prod  
3️⃣ Using **Environment Variables**           \-  export SPRING\_PROFILES\_ACTIVE=prod

**If no profile is active, Spring Boot loads:**

* **`application.properties`**  
* **`application.yml`**

**If a profile is active, it loads:**

1. **`application-{profile}.properties`**  
2. **`application.properties`**

# Microservices

### **Microservices**

Microservices architecture in **Spring Boot** is a way of designing applications as a **collection of loosely coupled, independently deployable services** that communicate via **REST APIs or messaging queues**.

### **Key Components of Spring Boot Microservices**

1. **Spring Boot** → Used to create individual microservices with embedded servers (Tomcat, Jetty).  
2. Spring Cloud 

### **Core Features in Spring Boot Microservices**

🔹 **Service Discovery** – Uses **Eureka Server** for dynamic service registration & lookup.  
🔹 **API Gateway** – Uses **Spring Cloud Gateway** or **Zuul** for routing, authentication, and load balancing.  
🔹 **Configuration Management** – Uses **Spring Cloud Config Server** to manage centralized configurations.  
🔹 **Inter-Service Communication** – Uses **REST (Feign Client)** or **Message Brokers (Kafka, RabbitMQ)**.  
🔹 **Resilience & Fault Tolerance** – Uses **Resilience4j/Hystrix** for circuit breaking.  
🔹 **Distributed Logging & Monitoring** – Uses **ELK Stack (Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana) & Zipkin** for tracing.

### **Advantages of Microservices in Spring Boot**

✅ **Scalability** – Services can be scaled independently.  
✅ **Flexibility** – Each microservice can use a different tech stack.  
✅ **Faster Deployment** – Independent deployment without affecting the whole system.  
✅ **Resilience** – Failure in one service doesn’t affect the entire application.

🔹 How do microservices communicate in Spring Boot?

---

**3\. What is an API Gateway ?**

\- **API Gateway** is a single entry point for client requests in a **microservices architecture**. It acts as a **reverse proxy**, handling requests and routing them to the appropriate microservices.

**Spring Cloud Gateway** is a popular API Gateway solution in **Spring Boot**.

### **Why is API Gateway Needed?**

🔹 **Centralized Entry Point** – Clients interact with **one endpoint** instead of multiple microservices.  
🔹 **Load Balancing** – Distributes traffic across multiple instances of microservices.  
🔹 **Authentication & Security** – Handles **JWT tokens, OAuth2, API keys** for authentication.  
🔹 **Request Routing** – Routes requests to the correct microservice.  
🔹 **Rate Limiting & Throttling** – Protects against excessive requests to prevent overload.  
🔹 **Monitoring & Logging** – Captures logs, traces, and analytics for requests.  
🔹 **Protocol Translation** – Converts **REST to gRPC, WebSockets, or GraphQL** if needed.

![][image49]

**Example:** Kong API Gateway, Netflix Zuul, NGINX.

 **7\. Design Patterns in Microservices ?**

🔹**Service Registry and Discover**y: Services automatically register in a central registry, allowing others to identify and interact with them dynamically.

🔹**API Gateway**: It acts as a customer entry point and forwards requests to appropriate microservices to provide additional functionality such as authentication and rate limits.

🔹**Circuit Breaker**: It monitors the availability of services and protects from failures by sending requests or by providing responses if service is unavailable.

🔹**CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation)**: It separates the read and write operations. Also, it optimizes each and every operation separately for efficiency.

🔹**Saga Pattern**: It manages distributed tasks by organizing a sequence of local transactions.

🔹**Database per service**: Each of the services has separate databases. This ensures data isolation and also enables scaling and individual development.

🔹**Asynchronous messaging**: Each services communicate with each other through message queues like Kafka or RabbitMQ.

#### **7\. What is Service Discovery in microservices?** Service Discovery helps services dynamically find each other.

* **Client-side discovery** – Services query a registry (e.g., Eureka).  
* **Server-side discovery** – A load balancer handles routing (e.g., Kubernetes, Consul).

The Service Discovery pattern **allows services to discover each other dynamically**. **Microservices register themselves with a service registry**, and clients or other services query this registry to locate the services they need to interact with

#### **9\. How do you secure microservices?**

* **Authentication & Authorization** – OAuth2, JWT, API Keys.  
* **Encryption** – HTTPS, TLS for secure data transfer.  
* **Rate Limiting & Throttling** – Prevent API abuse.  
* **Security Gateway** – API Gateway for authentication & access control.


#### **10\. What is Circuit Breaker Pattern?**

#### **prevents repeated failures** in microservices.

* If a service fails, further calls are blocked temporarily. ( based on a threshold )  
* Example implementation: **Resilience4j**, **Hystrix**.

![][image50]

#### **12\. What is CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation)?** CQRS separates read (`Query`) and write (`Command`) operations using different models.

* **Improves performance** by optimizing queries separately.  
* **Used with Event Sourcing** to track state changes.

#### **13\. What tools are used for monitoring microservices?**

* **Logging** – ELK Stack (Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana), Fluentd. log4j  
* **Tracing** – OpenTelemetry, Zipkin, Jaeger.  
* **Metrics** – Prometheus, Grafana.

#### **14\. Sidecar Pattern in Microservices? With Service mesh ( communication between services )**  **\-** **runs auxiliary tasks** alongside a microservice.

* Used in **Service Mesh** (e.g., Istio, Envoy).   
* **Hystrix \-  tolerate failure and latency** it is based on **circuit breaker pattern \-** 

  Prevents cascading failures: Hystrix prevents failures from spreading from one service to another

* Handles **logging, monitoring, security,** and **networking** independently.  
* Handles **Retry logic**

![][image51]

![][image52]

#### **Service mesh ( lots of microservice and communicating between services )**

A Service Mesh manages microservices communication, security, and monitoring.  
**Popular tools:** Istio, Linkerd, Consul.

![][image53]

#### **SAGA Pattern ( distributed Transaction )**

SAGA **splits a large transaction into multiple small transactions** that are handled by individual microservices. If a step fails, compensating transactions are executed to undo changes.

#### **16\. How do you deploy microservices in Kubernetes and Docker ?**

1. **Containerize the services** using Docker. ( dockerFile )  
2. **Deploy using Kubernetes** ( `kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml` ).  
3. **Use Helm charts** for managing configurations.  
4. **Manage communication** using Ingress, Service Mesh (Istio).  
5. **Monitor with Prometheus \+ Grafana.**

#### **20\. What is Blue-Green Deployment in Microservices?**

It is a deployment strategy where: **Two separate environments (Blue & Green) run simultaneously.**

* **Blue Environment**  → Active, The currently **live** (production) version.  
* **Green** **Environment** → **New version**, tested before switching traffic ( deployed and tested in parallel )  
* **Switch Traffic** → Once verified, **traffic is switched from Blue to Green**  
              (e.g., **via load balancer or service mesh** ).  
* **Rollback (if needed)** → If issues arise, traffic is routed back to Blue.

Reduces downtime and rollback risk.

#### **20\. Rolling Deployment (Default) Deployment in Microservices?**

**Gradually replaces old version pods with new versions pods.** 

* Ensures **zero downtime** but rollback may take time.


#### **21\. Canary Deployment**

* **Gradually shifts a small percentage of traffic to the new version before full rollout.**  
* Helps detect issues early before affecting all users.

#### **22\. How does Microservices communication**

* Microservices can communicate asynchronously using message queues, like apache kafka  
* Synchronously use HTTP/HTTPS requests

# Kafka

[https://debonair-bus-1a6.notion.site/Kafka-1af5c8b7e93580918aefe7dbda7f5072](https://debonair-bus-1a6.notion.site/Kafka-1af5c8b7e93580918aefe7dbda7f5072)

**Kafka**

Apache Kafka is a distributed event streaming platform designed for high-throughput, fault-tolerant, and scalable message processing. It is used for:

* **Real-time data processing**  
* Log aggregation  
* **Event-driven architectures**  
* **Messaging between microservices**  
* Data streaming and analytics

### **2\. Explain Kafka’s architecture.**

Kafka's architecture consists of:

1. **Producer** – **Publishes** messages to topics.

2. **Broker** – **Stores** and **distributes messages** across **partitions**.

3. **Topic** – A logical channel where messages are written.

4. **Partition** – A subset of a topic enabling parallel processing of messages.

5. **Consumer** – Reads messages from topics.

6. **Consumer Group** – A group of consumers reading from partitions.

7. **Zookeeper** – Manages Kafka metadata, leader election, and configurations.

**6\. What is a Broker in Kafka?**

* A broker is a **Kafka server** that runs in a **Kafka cluster**. 

* It **receives messages** from producers, **assigns offsets** to them, and **commits the messages to storage on disk**.

* It also services consumers, **responding to fetch requests for partitions** and  
  **responding with the messages that have been published**.

**3\. What does follower and leader in Kafka mean?**

* Partitions are created in Kafka based on consumer groups and offset.  
* One server in the partition serves as the leader, and one or more servers act as a follower  
* The leader assigns itself tasks that read and write partition requests  
* Followers follow the leader and replicate all the messages.

### **4\. How does Kafka handle consumer failure?**

* Kafka **re-assigns partitions** to other consumers in the group.  
* Consumer offsets are **committed periodically** to ensure no duplicate processing.  
* Consumers use **rebalance strategies** to redistribute partitions dynamically.

### **5\. What is Kafka’s ISR (In-Sync Replicas)?**

ISR refers to replicas that are up-to-date with the leader’s log.

* If a replica falls behind, it is removed from ISR.  
* Kafka elects a new leader from ISR in case of failure.

**6\. What is the role of ZooKeeper in Kafka?**

* ZooKeeper is used for **managing and coordinating Kafka brokers**.   
* It serves as a centralized service for maintaining configuration information, naming, providing distributed synchronization, and providing group services.   
* ZooKeeper keeps track of the status of Kafka cluster nodes, Kafka topics, and partitions.

**1\.** **ACID properties**

1️⃣ **Atomicity** – Transaction is **all or nothing**. No partial completion.  
2️⃣ **Consistency** – Database **remains valid** before & after the transaction.  
3️⃣ **Isolation** – Transactions do **not interfere** with each other.  
4️⃣ **Durability** – Committed changes are **permanent** even after failures.

✅**Example:** Bank transfer should ensure both debit and credit occur together (Atomicity).

2\. **Delete** vs **Truncate** vs **Drop**

| Delete | Truncate | Drop |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Specific rows | Deletes whole table but keeps structure( All rows Deleted ) | Drops entire table along with structure |
| Can be Rolled back  ( with ROLLBACK  ) | No rollback | No rollback |
| Speed slow | Fast  | Very Fast |
| DML | DDL | DDL |

DELETE FROM employees WHERE id \= 10;  \-- Removes one row  
TRUNCATE TABLE employees;  \-- Removes all rows  
DROP TABLE employees;  \-- Deletes entire table

**3\. DML** vs **DCL** vs **DDL**

| DML | DDL | DCL | TCL |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Deals with Data. | Deals with structure of DB | Deals with access control and permission to DB | Deals with Transactions |
| **Insert Update  Select  Delete** | **Create table Alter table Drop, Truncate table Create Schema** | **GRANT REVOKE** | **BEGIN COMMIT ROLLBACK** |

Transactions are sequences of operations treated as a single unit of work.

5\. **Joins**

  **\- Combines records from multiple tables** **based on** a related **common column** between those tables.

| Join | Desc |
| :---- | :---- |
| INNER | **Combine and return Matching rows from both tables** ( Rows with no match in either table are excluded ) |
| LEFT | **Combines All** **records** from the **left table** and matching rows from the right table. If there's no match in the right table, the columns from the right table will have **`NULL`** values |
| RIGHT | **Combine All records** from the **right table** and matching rows from the left table. |
| FULL (OUTER) | **Combine All records** from **both tables**If there's no match in either table, the columns from the missing table will have `NULL` values  |
| CROSS JOIN( Cartesian product ) | Returns **every possible combination** of rows from both tables.If table A has 3 rows and table B has 4 rows, the cross join will result in 3 \* 4 \= 12 rows. |
| Self JOIN | Joining a table to itself  |

Joins \- **1️⃣ INNER JOIN (Only Matching Records)**

**2️⃣ LEFT JOIN (All Left Table \+ Matching Right Table)**

**SELECT** e.id, e.name, d.dept\_name  
**FROM** Employees e  
**LEFT JOIN** Departments d **ON** e.dept\_id \= d.dept\_id;

If there's no match in the right table, the columns from the right table will have **`NULL`** values

**3️⃣ RIGHT JOIN (All Right Table \+ Matching Left Table)**  
**✅ Returns all departments, even if no employees belong to them.**

**SELECT** e.id, e.name, d.dept\_name  
**FROM** Employees e  
**RIGHT JOIN** Departments d **ON** e.dept\_id \= d.dept\_id; 

**4️⃣ FULL OUTER JOIN (All Records from Both Tables)**  
**✅ Returns all employees and all departments, even if there’s no match.**

**SELECT** e.id, e.name, d.dept\_name  
**FROM** Employees e  
**FULL OUTER JOIN** Departments d   
**ON** e.dept\_id \= d.dept\_id;

**5️⃣ CROSS JOIN (Cartesian Product)**  
**✅ Returns every possible combination of employees and departments.**

**SELECT** e.name, d.dept\_name   
**FROM** Employees e  
**CROSS JOIN** Departments d;

9\. **Composite Key**

A **composite key** is a **primary key that consists of two or more columns** to uniquely identify a row in a table. It is used when a single column is not sufficient to ensure uniqueness.

10\. **Group by**  
 \- **Groups identical records and is used with aggregate functions** (`SUM`, `COUNT`, etc.) to perform calculations on each group rather than on the entire dataset.

### **Rules for Using `GROUP BY` and `HAVING` in SQL**

#### **1\. `GROUP BY` Clause Rules:**

* Used to **group rows** that have the same values in specified columns.  
* Every column in the `SELECT` clause **must** be either:  
  * A grouped column (listed in `GROUP BY`).  
  * An aggregate function (`COUNT()`, `SUM()`, `AVG()`, etc.).  
* Cannot use column aliases in `GROUP BY`.

#### **2\. `HAVING` Clause Rules:**

* Used to filter grouped results **after aggregation**.  
* Can **only** use aggregate functions (`COUNT()`, `SUM()`, etc.) or grouped columns.  
* Cannot reference column aliases from the `SELECT` clause.

11\. **Normalization :**  
\- To reduce redundancy and improve data integrity.  
  1NF \- Atomic values ( no multiple values in a field )  
  2NF \-	No partial dependencies.  
  3NF \- No transitive dependencies.  
  BCNF \- Stronger version of 3NF

12: **What is database sharding?**

Sharding **horizontally partitions** data across multiple servers to improve performance.

#### **Example:**

* **Shard 1**: Customers with ID 1-5000  
* **Shard 2**: Customers with ID 5001-10000

**\- WHERE \- Filters rows before any grouping** takes place.  
\- **HAVING \- Filters grouped rows** after the GROUP BY has been applied.

**15\. What are indexes, and why are they used?**  
**Indexes are database objects that improve query performance** by **allowing faster retrieval of rows**.   
They function like a book’s index, making it quicker to find specific data without scanning the entire table. However, indexes require additional storage and can slightly slow down data modification operation

**16**. **What is the difference between ROW\_NUMBER() and RANK()?**  
**ROW\_NUMBER**(): Assigns a unique number to each row regardless of ties.  
**RANK**(): Assigns the same number to tied rows and leaves gaps for subsequent ranks.  
Example:

**SELECT Name, ROW\_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY Salary DESC) AS RowNum**    
**FROM Employees;**

**17\. What is the difference between clustered and non-clustered indexes?**

**1\. Clustered Index:**  
Organizes the physical data in the table itself in the order of the indexed column(s).  
A table can have only one clustered index.  
Improves range queries and queries that sort data.  
Example: If EmployeeID is the clustered index, the rows in the table are stored physically sorted by EmployeeID.

**2\. Non-Clustered Index:**  
Maintains a separate structure that contains a reference (or pointer) to the physical data in the table.  
A table can have multiple non-clustered indexes.  
Useful for specific query conditions that aren’t related to the primary ordering of the data.  
Example: A non-clustered index on LastName allows fast lookups by last name even if the table is sorted by another column.

15\. **Prepared Statements** 

Allows you to execute SQL queries efficiently **by precompiling the query and reusing it multiple times** with **different parameters.** 

**PREPARE  find\_user (int)   AS**  
**SELECT  \*  FROM   users   WHERE   id \= $1; // parameterized**

**EXECUTE  find\_user(42);**

#### Advantages of Prepared Statements

1. **Performance Improvement:** The query is parsed and planned once, saving computation time for repeated executions.  
2. **SQL Injection Prevention: User inputs are treated as parameters**, reducing the risk of injection attacks.  
3. **Code Reusability:** The same query can be executed multiple times with different values.

# React

**Differentiate between state and props.**

* **State** is a local data storage that is mutable and managed within a component.   
* **Props** (short for properties) are read-only attributes passed from parent to child components to configure or customize them.

**What are React Hooks?**

* Introduced in React 16.8, Hooks are functions that let developers use state and other React features in functional components, eliminating the need for class-based components.

**useState Hook.**

* `useState` Hook allows functional components to have state variables. It returns an array with the current state value and a function to update it. 

**useEffect Hook**

* `useEffect` you perform side effects in functional components, such as **data fetching**, **subscriptions**, or **manually changing the DOM**. It runs **after every render by defaul**t but **can be controlled with dependency arrays**

**useMemo Hook**

* `useMemo` you perform side effects in functional components, such as **data fetching**, **subscriptions**, or **manually changing the DOM**. It runs **after every render by defaul**t but **can be controlled with dependency arrays.**

 

**Explain the concept of lifting state up in React.**

* Lifting state up involves **moving the state to the closest common ancestor of components that need to share or synchronize data,** ensuring a single source of truth**. ( Moving useState up in parent that also needs the same data )**

**higher-order components (HOCs)?**

* **Answer: HOCs are functions that take a component and return a new component, allowing code reuse, logic, and bootstrap abstraction**

**Describe the Context API in React.**

* The Context API allows for **global state management** by providing a way to **pass data through the component tree** without having to pass props down manually at every level

**What is the purpose of keys in React lists?**

* **Answer:** Keys help React identify which items have changed, been added, or removed in a list. They should be unique among siblings to optimize rendering performance. 

**What is prop drilling, and how can it be avoided?**

* Prop drilling refers to the process of passing data through multiple nested components that do not need it, just to reach a component

**How do you optimize performance in a React application?**

* **Answer:** Performance can be optimized by techniques such as code splitting, lazy loading, memoization using `React.memo`, using the `useCallback` and `useMemo` Hooks, and avoiding unnecessary renders

**What is lexical scope in JavaScript?**

* The way that variables are resolved based on their location, This means that **functions have access to variables in their own scope and the outer (lexical) scopes.**

     **What is the difference between `==` and `===` in JavaScript?**

* **Answer:** `==` is the abstract equality operator that compares two values for equality after converting both values to a common type (type coercion). `===` is the strict equality operator that compares both the value and the type without performing type conversion. 

     **What is a closure in JavaScript?**

* A closure **is a function that retains access to its lexical scope**, even when the function is executed outside that scope. This allows the function to access variables from its containing scope.  
* Child functions to keep access of variables of the parent’s scope even after they are executed.

**Explain hoisting in JavaScript.**

* **Default behavior of moving func and variables declarations to the top of the current scope**. This means that **variable** and **function** declarations are processed before any code is executed. However, **only the declarations are hoisted**, not the initializations.

    **What are arrow functions, and how do they differ from regular functions?**

*  Arrow functions are a **concise syntax for writing function expressions** introduced in ES6.  
  They differ from regular functions in that they do not have their own `this`, `arguments`, `super`, or `new.target` bindings. As a result, they inherit `this` from the enclosing scope.


**Explain the concept of promises in JavaScript.**

* A promise **represents eventual completion or failure of an asynchronous operation**. It allows you to attach callbacks for handling success (`.then()`) or failure (`.catch()`) of the asynchronous operation.

**What is the purpose of the `async` and `await` keywords?**

* **`async`** keyword **declares an asynchronous function**, **which returns a promise**.   
* **`await`** keyword is **used inside `async` functions to pause execution** **until the awaited promise is resolved or rejected**, simplifying the chaining of promises

**What is the event loop in JavaScript?**

* The event loop is a mechanism that **allows JavaScript to perform non-blocking operations** by offloading tasks to the browser, **enabling asynchronous code execution**.  
* **It continuously checks the call stack and the message queue**, executing tasks from the queue when the stack is empty.

**What is event delegation in JavaScript?**

* Event delegation is a technique where a parent element listens for events on its child elements using `event.target`.

![][image58]

---

**What is the difference between synchronous and asynchronous JavaScript?**

* **Synchronous: Executes code line by line.**  
* **Asynchronous: Executes non-blocking operations like API calls, timers, etc.**

Eg.   
1\. The **setTimeout function is executed**.  
2\. It schedules the callback `() => console.log("Middle")` to run **after 1000ms**.  
3\. The callback is sent to the **Web APIs (or Timer Queue in Node.js)**.

4\.  After **1000ms**, the `setTimeout` callback (`console.log("Middle")`)  
    callback is **moved to the Callback Queue**.

5\. The **Event Loop**  checks if the existing Call Stack is empty.

* Once the existing synchronous code finishes executing,   
  1\. the **callback from the queue is pushed onto the Call Stack**.  
  2\. The callback (`console.log("Middle")`) is executed from the Call Stack.

* Output: **Hello** (after 1 second).

Callback method moves to \> **Callback queue** \> **Call stack** ( managed by **event loop** ) \> **execute**

**What is the difference between `call()`, `apply()`, and `bind()`?**

* **`call()`: Calls a function with a specified `this` value and arguments.**  
* **`apply()`: Similar to `call()`, but passes arguments as an array.**  
* **`bind()`: Returns a new function with `this` bound.**

# NodeJs Express Angular

**1\.  Event loop \-**   
\-  It uses a single-threaded event loop model.  
\-  The event-loop is the main processing model.  
\-  Node.js retrieves the incoming requests and adds those to the Event Queue   
\-  The requests are then passed one by one through the Event loop.

\-  The Event Loop processes simple requests (non-blocking operations), such as I/O Polling, and returns the responses to the corresponding clients

A single thread from the Thread Pool is assigned to a single complex request. This thread is responsible for completing a particular blocking request by accessing external resources, such as computation, database, file system, etc.

Once the task is carried out completely, the response is sent to the Event Loop that sends that response back to the client.

**Event loops handle asynchronous callbacks in Node.js**. It is the foundation of Node.js's non-blocking input/output in Node.js, making it one of the most important environmental features.

**Angular** 

**1\.** Introduced to create **single page applications.** It used HTML syntax to express components clearly.

**2. Advantages of Angular**

* **MVC architecture**: Angular is a full-fledged MVC framework. It also offers **bi-directional data flow** and **updates the real DOM**.   
* **Two-way data binding:** Synchronizes data between the model and the view automatically.  
* **Modularization**: Angular consists of different design patterns like **components, directives, pipes,** and services, which help in the smooth creation of applications.  
* **Dependency injection**: Components dependent on other components can be easily worked around using this feature.

### **2\. What is data binding? Which type of data binding does Angular deploy?**

Data binding allows any user to manipulate Web page elements using a Web browser. It uses dynamic HTML. We use data binding in web pages that contain **interactive components** such as **forms**, calculators, tutorials. **Angular provides a function Data Binding** which helps us to have an almost **real-time reflection of the input given by the user** i.e. it creates a connection between Model and View.

**Angular uses two-way binding.** any changes in the model state are reflected in the UI state. This allows the framework to connect the DOM(view) to the Model data via the controller. However, this approach affects performance since every DOM change must be tracked.

### **1️⃣ One-Way Data Binding**

**This means data flows in a single direction —\>** either from the **component to the view** or flow from the **view to the component.**

#### **(a) Interpolation (`{{ }}`)**

* **Used to display component properties inside HTML.**  
* **One-way binding from component → view.**  
* \<p\>Welcome, {{ username }}\</p\>

#### **(b) Property Binding (`[property]`)**

* Binds a property of an HTML element to a component property.  
* One-way binding from **component → view**.  
* \<img \[src\]="imageUrl"\>

#### **(c) Event Binding (`(event)`)**

* Used to handle user events (e.g.,c clicks, input changes).  
* One-way binding from **view → component**.  
* \<button (click)="handleClick()"\>Click me\</button\>

### **2️⃣ Two-Way Data Binding (`[(ngModel)]`)**

* **Allows bi-directional binding between component and view.**  
* **Uses `ngModel` directive (requires `FormsModule` in `app.module.ts`).**  
* **![][image61]**  
  Here **changes in the input field update the username property** and vice versa.

**![][image62]**

### 

### **4\. Differences between one-way binding and two-way binding**

* **Property Binding:** Similar to Java, **variables defined in the parent class** can be **inherited by the child class** that is **templates** in this case.   
  The only difference between Interpolation and Property binding is that we **should not store non-string values in variables while using interpolation**. So if we have to store Boolean or other data types then use Property Binding.  
* **Interpolation Binding:** Angular interpolation is used to **display a component property in the respective view template with double curly braces syntax.** Interpolation is used to transfer properties mentioned in component class to be reflected in its template.

# Rest API & HTTP methods

1\. What are **HTTP methods** ?

\- Define the type of operation that is performed on a resource in a RESTful API. 

\- **GET** \- Retrieve data from the server. 

\- **POST** \-   Create a new resource.

\- **PUT** \-   **Update an existing resource** (or **create if not exists / Replace it)**.

\- **PATCH** \-   **Partially update** an existing resource.

\- **DELETE** \-   Delete a resource from the server.

\- **OPTIONS** \-   **Get supported HTTP methods** for a resource.

\- **HEAD** \- Retrieve response headers without the body.

2\. **GET** vs **POST** 

| Feature | GET | POST |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Purpose | Fetch data from server | Create a new resource |
| Idempotent | Yes | No |
| Request body | Not used ( send through URL ) | Uses request body to send data. |
| Caching | Can be Cached | No cached by default |

3\. **PUT** vs **PATCH**

| Feature | PUT | PATCH |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Purpose | **Replace the entire resource** | **Partially update the resource** |
| Idempotent | Yes | No |
| Request body | Full object required | Only the fields to be updated. |

4\.  **Stateless behaviour**

\- each request from a client to the server must contain all the information necessary for the server to understand and fulfill that request independently of any previous requests.

5. HTTP methods are **Idempotent**

**\-** A method is idempotent if **calling it multiple times** produces the **same result**.

 \- GET \- Fetching data multiple times does not change it.

 \- PUT \- Updating a resource with the same data is ok.

 \- DELETE \- Deleting the same resource multiple times gives the same result.

**Non**\-**Idempotent**

\- POST \- Creating a new resource multiple times results in multiple records.

\- PATCH \- 

6\. **How do you secure a REST API**

**\-** JWT \- Token based authentication.

\- HTTPS \- Encrypt communication to prevent data leaks.

\- Rate Limiting \- Putting limits on requests to prevent API abuse.

\- API Keys, OAuth 2.0 \- Standard Authorization framework.

7\. What is **CORS** ?

\- Cross-origin resource sharing, allows web applications to access resources from different domains.

\- By default \- browsers block cross-origin requests for security purposes.

\- CORS headers like  Access-Control-Allow-Origin  allow cross-domain access.

![][image64]

8\. **REST vs SOAP**

| Feature | REST | SOAP |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Protocol | **uses JSON/XML data over HTTP** | **XML over HTTP, TCP, SMTP** |
| Lightweight | Yes | No ( more overhead ) |
| Performance | Fast | Slow due to XML parsing |
| security | Relies on HTTPS | Supports WS-Security |

9\. HTTP status codes.

| Success | Error |
| :---- | :---- |
| **200 200** : Ok \- Request Success ( GET, PUT, DELETE ) | **400 Bad Request** \- Invalid request syntax  |
| 201: Created, Resource created successfully ( POST ) | **401 Unauthorized** \- Authentication required |
| 204: No content returned | **403 Forbidden** \- Server refuses the request |
| 500 : Internal server error 503 : Server unavailable \- server down | **404 Not Found** \- Resource does not exist. |

11\. How does REST API support **Caching**

\- Caching to improve performance using **cache-control headers**.

Eg. Response Header: 

**Cache-Control: max-age=3600**  ( tells browser to cache the response for 1 hr )

12\. What are **Websockets** ? vs **REST API**

\- allow **real-time bi-directional communication** ( **chat apps** )

\- Rest API \- use **stateless request-response model** mainly for CRUD.

# GraphQL

### **What is GraphQL?**

GraphQL is a **query language** and **runtime** for APIs, that allows clients to request exactly the data they need. It provides a **flexible and efficient** alternative to traditional REST APIs.

**Key Features of GraphQL:**

1. **Client-Specified Queries** – **Clients can request specific fields instead of receiving a fixed set of**  
                                                     **data**.  
2. **Single Endpoint** – Unlike REST, which has multiple endpoints for different resources,  
                                     **GraphQL uses a single endpoint** (e.g., **`/graphql`**).  
3. **Strongly Typed Schema** – APIs are defined using a **GraphQL schema** that enforces type safety.  
4. **Real-Time Data** – GraphQL supports **subscriptions**, **enabling real-time updates.**  
5. **No Over-fetching or Under-fetching** – **Clients get only the necessary data**, improving performance.

# Hibernate JPA ORM

1\. What is Hibernate and how is it related to JPA ?  
\- **Hibernate is an ORM** ( Object relational mapping ) framework that **simplifies database interactions** by mapping **java objects to database tables**.

\- **JPA** ( Java persistence API ) is a standard specification for ORM in Java. Hibernate is one of the most popular JPA implementations.

🔹 **JPA \= Specification** (Interface)  
🔹 **Hibernate \= Implementation** (ORM Framework)

2\. **Core components of Hibernate ?**  
\- **Transaction** \- Manages database transactions ( **commit** and **rollback** )  
\- **Query** \- Used to execute queries.  
\- **Session** \- A lightweight object used for interacting with DB.  
\- **SessionFactory** \- **Heavyweight** object that **manages sessions** ( created once per application )  
\- **Configuration** \- Reads hibernate.cfg.xml or annotations for DB settings.  
---

**3\. Types of caching in hibernate ?**

1\. ✅ **First-Level Cache (L1 Cache)**   
  \- Enabled by default.  
  \- Works **per session** ( **session** object )  
  \- Hibernate **stores objects in memory** to avoid repeated DB queries.

2\. ✅ **Second-Level Cache (L2 Cache)**  
  \- Works per application ( at the level of **SessionFactory** )  
  \- Requires **external providers like Redis**  
  \- **Improves performance** across **multiple sessions**.

3\. ✅ **Query Cache** \-  
 \- **Stores query results** for repeated queries.  
 \- Works along with 2nd Level Cache.

4\. **save()** vs **persist()** vs **update()** vs **merge()**

| Method | Works with  | Returns | When to use |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **save()** | New entities | Identifier | Inserts the object into DB. |
| **persist()** | New entities | void | Same as save() but follows JPA rules. |
| **update()** | Detached entities | void | Updates an existing object in DB. |
| **merge()** | Detached entities | Merged object | Merges changes from a detached object into the persistence context. |

**1️⃣ `save()` \-    session.save()    ( Hibernate only )**  
**\- return generated ID for new entity**  
**\- If the entity doesn't exist (i.e., no corresponding record in the DB), it inserts the entity into the database.**

**2️⃣ `persist()`  \-  em.persist()   ( JPA )**  
**\- Similar to `save()`, but `persist()` only works for new entities that do not yet exist in the database.**  
**\- It does not return the ID (only `save()` returns the generated ID).**  
**\-** If the entity already exists (i.e., it has a primary key), it will throw an exception (typically `javax.persistence.EntityExistsException`)

**3️⃣ `update()` Method (Hibernate only)  \- session.update()**  
**\- If the entity exists (i.e., has a matching primary key), it will update the corresponding database record.**  
**\-** If the entity does not exist, an exception will be thrown (`org.hibernate.ObjectNotFoundException`).  
**\-** It can cause data loss in some cases, especially if the entity is detached and the update is not done carefully.

**4️⃣ `merge()` Method (JPA & Hibernate) \- em.merge()**

* **If the entity is detached (i.e., it was previously retrieved or modified outside of the current session), `merge()` will reconnect it with the current session and return a managed entity instance.**  
* If the **entity is new,** it behaves like **`persist()` and inserts the entity** into the database.  
* If the **entity already exists**, it **updates() the entity with changes** from the detached instance.  
* **Returns a new entity instance (which is managed by the session).**

**5\. Transactions** in Hibernate **?**  
It manages transactions using **beginTransaction(), commit() and rollback().** Transactions ensure consistency in case of failures.  
![][image68]

6\. Fetching strategies   
✅ **Lazy Loading (default)** – Loads data only when accessed (`@OneToMany(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)`).  
✅ **Eager Loading** – Loads related data **immediately** (`@OneToMany(fetch = FetchType.EAGER)`).

7\. What is **@Entity** annotation in hibernate ?  
\- `@Entity` marks a class as a **JPA entity** (**mapped to a DB table**). Without `@Entity`, Hibernate ignores the class.  
![][image69]

8\. What is `@OneToMany` and `@ManyToOne` mapping in Hibernate?

1. **@OneToMany \-  1 department many employees ( dept for every Employee )**  
2. **@ManyToOne \- Each employee belongs to 1 department. ( Employees inside a dept )**

   **![][image70]![][image71]**  
     
   

**9\. Common performance issues in Hibernate ? How to optimize**

**🚀** Use **batch processing (`hibernate.jdbc.batch_size`).**  
**🚀** Enable **second-level caching (EhCache / L2 Cache).**  
**🚀** Use **Lazy Loading to avoid unnecessary joins.**  
**🚀** Optimize **HQL queries (use indexes).**

**10\. HQL**

- **HQL (Hibernate Query Language)** is an **object-oriented query** language in Hibernate.  
- It **operates on entities** (objects) instead of raw database tables.  
- ![][image72]

11\. **Session()** vs **SessionFactory()**

![][image73]

12\. Different **states of an entity** in Hibernate ?

1️⃣ **Transient** – The object is **not associated with Hibernate** and **not persisted** in the DB.  
2️⃣ **Persistent** – The object is **associated with Hibernate** (`session.save()`) and **synced with the DB**.  
3️⃣ **Detached** – The object was **persistent** but the session is now **closed** (modifications won't reflect in the DB).

13\. **Advantages of Hibernate** ?  
✅ **Eliminates Boilerplate Code** – No need for manually writing SQL queries for CRUD operations.  
✅ **Database Independence** – Works with **multiple databases** (MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, etc.).  
✅ **Automatic Table Mapping** – Uses annotations/XML for mapping Java classes to DB tables.  
✅ **Caching Support** – Improves performance with **first-level** and **second-level** caching.  
✅ **HQL (Hibernate Query Language)** – Allows writing database-independent queries.  
✅ **Lazy Loading & Eager Loading** – Controls when related data is fetched.

**2\. What is DockerFile and How to create a docker image ?**

A **Dockerfile** is a script that contains instructions to build a **Docker image**. It defines the base image, dependencies, environment variables, and the command to run the application.

---

\# Use an official JDK runtime as a base image  
**FROM  openjdk:17-jdk-slim**

\# Set the working directory in the container  
**WORKDIR   /app**

\# Copy the built JAR file to the container  
**COPY   target/myapp.jar   app.jar**

\# Command to run the application  
**ENTRYPOINT** \["java", "-jar", "app.jar"\]

---

**Build the Docker Image** Run the following command in the project directory:  
**\> docker build \-t my-java-app .**

**Run the Container**  
**\> docker run \-p 8080:8080 my-java-app . ( container port : hostport )**

---

**IMP:**

* **`Dockerfile` automates the creation of Docker images.**  
* **Uses `FROM` to define the base image (e.g., `openjdk`).**  
* **`COPY` transfers the JAR file into the container.**  
* **`ENTRYPOINT` specifies how to run the Java application.**  
* **`docker build` creates an image, `docker run` starts a container.**

**Deployment Pipeline \-**  
Define the GitHub Actions Workflow (`deploy.yml`)

 name: CI/CD Pipeline for Spring Boot

 on:  
  push:  
    branches:  
      \- main  
  pull\_request:  
    branches:  
      \- main

 jobs:  
  build:  
    name: Build & Test  
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:  
      \- name: Checkout Code  
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      \- name: Set up JDK 17  
        uses: actions/setup-java@v3  
        with:  
          distribution: 'temurin'  
          java-version: '17'

      \- name: Build with Maven  
        run: mvn clean package \-DskipTests

      \- name: Run Tests  
        run: mvn test

      \- name: Upload Artifact  
        uses: actions/upload-artifact@v3  
        with:  
          name: spring-boot-app  
          path: target/\*.jar

  deploy:  
    name: Deploy to Server  
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest  
    needs: build

    steps:  
      \- name: Download Artifact  
        uses: actions/download-artifact@v3  
        with:  
          name: spring-boot-app

      \- name: Deploy to Server  
        env:  
          SSH\_PRIVATE\_KEY: ${{ secrets.SSH\_PRIVATE\_KEY }}  
          SERVER\_USER: ${{ secrets.SERVER\_USER }}  
          SERVER\_HOST: ${{ secrets.SERVER\_HOST }}  
          DEPLOY\_PATH: "/home/${{ secrets.SERVER\_USER }}/app"

        run: |  
          echo "$SSH\_PRIVATE\_KEY" \> private\_key && chmod 600 private\_key  
          scp \-i private\_key \-o StrictHostKeyChecking=no \*.jar $SERVER\_USER@$SERVER\_HOST:$DEPLOY\_PATH/app.jar  
          ssh \-i private\_key \-o StrictHostKeyChecking=no $SERVER\_USER@$SERVER\_HOST \<\< 'EOF'  
            cd $DEPLOY\_PATH  
            pkill \-f 'java \-jar' || true  
            nohup java \-jar app.jar \> log.txt 2\>&1 &  
          EOF
